newsitem.title: USA: Sequa says 2 Pratt claims dismissed.
newsitem.headline: Sequa says 2 Pratt claims dismissed.

text.p: Sequa Corp said Wednesday a federal district court in Delaware has dismissed two royalty claims filed against its Chromalloy Gas Turbine subsidiary by United Technologies Corp's Pratt & Whitney unit.
Sequa said the court rejected Pratt's claims for double royalties on jet engine component repairs under multiple contracts.
But in its statement, Pratt & Whitney said the court ruled in its favor in deciding Chromally violated a licensing agreement by failing to pay fees to the jet engine building.
Pratt & Whitney also said "Chromalloy has agreed to pay the back royalties it owes with interest. The final sum is expected to be several million dollars."
An attorney for Sequa said Pratt & Whitney's statement was "flat wrong."
A Pratt & Whitney spokesman said he "did not dispute" Sequa's statement that the court dismissed the two claims.
In its statement, Sequa said the two companies agreed, following the rulings, to resolve specific issues that had been in contention in the suit.

"As part of the agreement to settle one dispute," Sequa said, "Pratt & Whitney has recognized Chromalloy's license to perform certain repairs Pratt had claimed were unauthorized, and Chromalloy agreed to pay Pratt royalties for these repairs. Pratt also agreed to dismiss related claims for patent and trademark infringement and unfair competition."

"In addition, the companies agreed to resolve several other disputes over royalties, and Pratt agreed to accept overpayments by Chromalloy under one contract as a credit against any underpayment by Chromalloy under another contract."

Chromalloy chairman, Martin Weinstein, said, "We are pleased by this partial resolution of our dispute pending in the Delaware court, and it remains our desire to resolve the rest of our contract disputes with Pratt."

Pratt & Whitney said the judge's finding that Chromalloy had violated its linense agreement came as part of a breach of contract action Pratt & Whitney filed. The remainin issues are anticipated to be tried later this year the U.S. District Court in Delaware.
It said the royalties at issue cover Chromalloy's use of cereamic coatings for jet engine airfoils and other patented processes.

The Delaware action is related to the recent Texas state court antitrust case in which the jury rejected Chromalloy's claim it had suffered monetary damage because of Pratt & Whitney's alleged monopolization of the jet engine repair business, the company said.
The jury also found Chromalloy had engaged in unfair competition, misappropriation of Pratt & Whitney data and fraudulent concealment.
The Texas court recently ruled that Chromalloy could not collect any damages from Pratt & Whitney or get an injunction.
